table.template.html.text: The Periodic Table of Cinematic Signs The 44 signs of Deleuze's cineosis as systematised by David Deamer, Deleuze's Cinema Books: Three Introductions to the Taxonomy of Images (Edinburgh UP, 2016). Each element is exemplified by a family of specific shots from the Moving Image Archive. Reading the table. Columns are Deamer's images. The movement-image runs from perception (zeroness) through affect (Firstness), action (Secondness) and thought (Thirdness). The three-digit code under each column is Deamer's Peircean combination (Fig. I.15): 111 affection, 211 impulse, 221 small-form action, 222 large-form action, 311 attraction, 321 inversion, 322 discourse, 331 dream, 332 recollection, 333 relation. The time-image follows Fig. I.20: 0 opsigns and sonsigns, 1 hyalosigns, 2 chronosigns, 3 noosigns, ∞ lectosigns. Rows. Each image is composed of two signs of composition and generated by one sign of genesis (bottom row). The time-image opens with its zeroness, split here into two elements: the opsign (a pure optical situation) and the sonsign (a pure sound situation). Deamer treats them as one sign; they are separated here because they differ in modality and a shot can be one without the other. The lectosign stands alone as the limit that closes the regime. The one-line gloss on each element is the caption of Deamer's own figure for that sign (Figs. II.01–II.44). The examples. The archive is public-domain educational, industrial, amateur, newsreel and early silent film, searched shot by shot with visual queries derived from the scenes Deamer analyses. None of it is the canon Deleuze cites. Each still is the matched frame of a single shot; hover or tap to play only that shot. Deleuze reminds us a film "is never made up of a single kind of image" (C1: 70): these are shots where the sign is dominant, not pure specimens. Difference and confidence. Hover an element to light up the three signs it is most often confused with. Each sheet opens with the test that decides between them. Each shot carries a reading: a solid bar for what the shot alone can show (capped by the sign's single-shot ceiling, ⌈ on the tile), a hatched bar for how far the reading goes if the surrounding sequence cooperates, and the rival sign's share in its own colour. A prompt is a bucket turned mouth-down into the sand: you speak into the ground and pump until something comes up. Every drill stroke births a new bucket. THE SIGNS (OF THE 45) MiMilieu The first sign of the large form: a fully determined geographical, historical and social situation (the Encompasser), laid out through establishing and extreme wide shots, whose characters' actions merely exemplify it. BiBinomial The second sign of the large form: the milieu splits into two opposed lines of force embodied by characters, and the film proceeds through duels (violent, romantic, political) converging on a final decisive one. ImImprint The genetic sign of the large form: a complex milieu is internalised by a character, accumulating as pressure until it explodes into action, and made visible through an emotional object that links the character to the situation. LlLimit of the large form action-image The first sign of composition of the discourse-image: the given milieu hides a question, and the character has to draw out that problem before any action can be a considered response rather than an explosive reaction. lab/slopfeeder.html.text: SLOPFEEDER BLACKTOP ↗ THE STUDIO ↗ THE CHAPTERS ↗ 28 frames · 6 source segments · 370 pieces cut out · against 35,995 archival shots THE READING THE SOURCE THE WORLD THE FRAMES THE BEATS THE ARCHIVE WHO THEY ARE FIGHTING The meme is a quarrel about one login page. Up top, the designer's four cartoon shapes, whose eyes follow your cursor and sulk at a wrong password. Below it, the developer answers with Ghost's stare: the masked passenger who turns and says nothing. The designer's answer is a grin. The joke is the gap between a picture that reacts to everything and a person who has to build it. SLOPFEEDER turns that gap into a siege, and the enemy is not people. Offshore is the render: the approved picture of how things should look, arriving as shellfire. Every shell is a change request ("Could you move it slightly left?"). The tide is production: "The sea has requested changes", "The tide found a bug". The wall is what the picture promised and the brick cannot keep. The skull-masked cook is the developer, and his stare is the only thing on the beach that doesn't move. He doesn't fight the render; he feeds the line that has to hold the wall while it lands. That is the title: the one who feeds people while the slop comes in. The Slopling, the tall thing that "grew up", is the generated work itself, which turns out able to carry a beam. To make the fight legible, give the render a face: the login page's four shapes, grown to the size of ships, standing off the coast with their eyes tracking the crew, as frame 178 already half does. They never fire at anyone; they only watch, and request changes. The archive comes in as testimony that none of this is new: field kitchens fed men under fire, crews hauled rope and timber on beaches, divers and pilots wore masks and stared through them. Under each tab are the archive's own versions of every piece and beat. lab/ludens/open-cut.html.text: LUDENS PUTT-OFF TENNIS OPEN CUT THE TABLE SLOPFEEDER THE REPUBLIC THE ODYSSEY NORSE HALF MOON THE SIGNS MENU OPEN CUT Golf and tennis at once, and an editor. Everyone sits around one round field of shots and takes turns. Your ball's line of flight is your cut: every free shot it crosses joins our one film, for as long as the ball is over it, and becomes yours. Claimed shots are walls for everyone. The film plays in the middle. Aim: drag back from your ball; the exact line, the shots it will cut and how they join appear, and stay. Adjust by dragging again or with the arrow keys. PREVIEW plays the proposed segment; CUT IT (Enter) commits. A fast putt cuts quickly through many shots; a slow one holds; the shot it comes to rest on holds longest. Each hole is a chapter; its flag is a shot the story stands on. Aim: drag back from the ball. The line, the shots it will cross and the cut it makes appear at once, and stay. Adjust by dragging again, or with the arrow keys (left/right turn, up/down power). lab/papers.html.text: CINEOSIS LAB · THE FILMS, WRITTEN UP Cineosis Papers Each film in the series as a short paper. Each one covers the questions the film puts to the archive, where those questions came from (a poem line, a treatment, a chapter's moods, a sign), what was measured, what it found, and what we are unsure of. The films show; these say what was shown and how far to trust it. What runs through all of them The archive answers questions; it does not volunteer. Everything a film shows was first a question, written by a person, a treatment, or a language model. A film inherits the vocabulary of whoever asked. The asker's words are not the poet's. In Where You Go When You Leave, a literal question shares 17% of its words with the line it was written for. The model added night 56 times; the poet said it 8 times. Feelings do not survive the search. Of 121 feelings listed in the poem's own suite data, 120 never reached a question. Symbols can be pictured, so they can be searched; feelings cannot. Machine closeness is compressed. For a typical moment the forty best matches differ by about 0.045. What decides between them is usually not the picture's meaning. A machine's sign is not a reading. 253 shots were read by a person; the rest carry a machine's guess, and a reader's sign is in the machine's top five only about half the time. The archive has a shape. It is mostly American educational, industrial and amateur film from the 1930s to the 1960s, mostly 4:3, and its voices are mostly men's: in the census of six lab films, character voices are 51 men to 9 women. lab/bolas/line-circle-dot.html.text: Bolas set 06 / 14 ← Screen Test Wink, Not Blink → THE OPERATIVE ARCHIVE · CINEOSIS LAB Line, circle, dot. Three elements every era of image-making has drawn. A line is time and the thread. A circle is the reel, the lens, the eye, the O. A dot is where attention rests: the bead, the reader. The whole identity, and Bolas with it, is made of nothing else. Why the small eyes went They were a spider's eight eyes True to the animal, but at any size below a hand they read as dots of dirt around a head, and they made the mark a cartoon. One dot does more A single dot inside the O can look anywhere, be anywhere on the line, be solid, hatched or empty. Everything the six eyes did, it does by position. The legs are behaviour The character keeps its legs and its face for when it performs. The mark never needs them: an O hanging on a line already is a spider, a reel, a pendulum, a plumb bob, an eye. The mark The mark A red hairline, a ring, one dot. Hung on its line, the O is Bolas, a reel, a lens, a plumb bob, an eye. A THE OPERATIVE ARCHIVE The ligature The O of the mark set beside an A drawn in the house serif. All ink except the thread. The Operative Archive The signature The name in the serif, and the mark hung, at the size of a full stop, over the i of Archive. The countdown The O as the leader circle. In motion the dot travels round the rim, ten to one, and the thread marks twelve o'clock. The playhead Laid on its side, the thread is a timeline, the shots are beads, and the mark is the reader standing on now. documented inferred unknown The certainty of the dot Centred and solid: documented. Off-centre and hatched: inferred. No dot at all: unknown, the O still open. One line, three states The same line, carrying the same shots as beads. Wound, it is the reel: the archive in storage. Pulled straight, it is the timeline: a film playing. Woven, it is the web: what the shots have to do with one another. The O travels it as the reader. Reel the archive wound on itself: everything kept, in the order it was made Line one film unwound: time, a playhead, shots in sequence Web the relations: the same shot in many films, readings that agree, questions that join now: reel the dot: where the reader is As timelines The same three elements are the interface for any film in the archive. Each shot is a bead; its dot says what is known about it; the O is the reader, wherever it is.

lab/bolas/screen-test.html.text: Bolas set 05 / 14 ← Operations Bible Line, Circle, Dot → THE OPERATIVE ARCHIVE · CINEOSIS LAB BOLAS SCREEN TEST Before an actor is cast they are filmed counting down, turning, reacting. This is Bolas's: inside the O of the archive, which is also the countdown circle at the head of every reel. Then the acting: one face rig, and three shots built the way hand-drawn animation is, from keys, breakdowns and in-betweens. THE RULES OF THE DETAILS RED IS ONLY THE THREAD The line Bolas hangs from, throws, cuts with. Never a leg, never a stripe, never part of a letter. Wherever red appears, an operation is happening. THE O IS A CIRCLE WITH A JOB The countdown, the lens, the reel, the abdomen. It is drawn as a ring, never filled, so something can always happen inside it. THE A IS ALL INK Its two legs stand; its crossbar is the ground line Bolas can stand on. GOLD IS A BEAD A caught voice or a person's reading, always a small round bead on the thread, never a fill. THE EYES DO THE ACTING Two big eyes with lids; six small eyes that work as brows and light gold when it reads. SMALL IS DRAWN, NOT SHRUNK At sixteen pixels every symbol is redrawn on the grid; the thread stays one pixel and stays red. THE COUNTDOWN, TEN TO ONE The O is the leader's circle. Each count is one beat of the screen test: Bolas drops into the circle and gives a different reading of the same frame, until one, and the cut. 2 SCREEN TEST · BOLAS · 02 · found it pause slow 2 · found it THE EXPRESSION SHEET A close-up: one head, twelve states. Lids, pupils, the six small eyes used as brows, the fangs, and the front pair of legs used as arms. Every state below is a key the animation can travel between. lab/bolas/sign-marks.html.text: Bolas set 01 / 14 ← Bolas → THE OPERATIVE ARCHIVE · CINEOSIS LAB Cineosis Sign Marks One master mark, then three ideas for each of the 45 signs the lab reads for, after Deleuze's cinema books as tabulated by David Deamer. Every mark is built from the same few parts, so the 45 read as one family and any of them can sit on a favicon, a card or a film slate. The parts FRAME the square: a shot, an interval, the evidence. RED LINE the operation: the cut, the playhead, a force acting. One red operation per mark; it may repeat, as a mark does. CELL solid is documented, hatched is inferred, empty is unknown. CIRCLE a centre: a face, a voice, a seed, a past. GOLD used once, in the signs where a person's own voice or face carries the sign. FAMILY CODE in the letter marks, the red stroke's angle says the family, so the symbol alone tells you which regime you are in. The master mark OA, the stroke as operation. Your mark: the A only stands when the red stroke completes it. The archive needs the operation to hold up. O as the frame, A as the archive. The same red runs through the O as a playhead and forms the A's stroke: one operation, two places. Oa 46 operative archive The 46th element. The archive itself as the cell the table was missing, with the stroke rule carried over from the sign marks. CINEOSIS unread, still cut The empty cell. For loading and missing states: the frame nobody has read yet, with the operation still running through it. The colour One colour carries the brand: Cue Red. It already means the operation in every film and room, the playhead and the cut, so it stays rare: one red operation in any view. Everything else is archive black and paper. Gold and lime keep the two meanings they have earned, and appear only when that meaning is there. Cue Red · #E0483A the operation: playhead, cut, the one red thing in a view Archive Black · #0B0A09 the ground of every film and room Paper · #F1F0EA the ground of print, papers and catalogue Voice Gold · #E8C070 only where a person speaks or reads Choice Lime · #C4F46A only where a person or a rule has chosen Data Grey · #A29D90 metadata, counts, captions The avatar: Cue Cue is a frame that walks: a square shot with one eye, on two legs, and one leg is red, exactly as the red stroke completes the A in OA. lab/bolas/system.html.text: Bolas set 03 / 14 ← Bolas Operations Bible → THE OPERATIVE ARCHIVE · CINEOSIS LAB BOLAS, AS A SYSTEM One mark that is a spider, two letters, a playhead and a measurement at once, drawn from the lab's most reused piece of film, and able to carry any production, any material and any scale. And because it can be drawn from data, the mark itself can be an operative image: each film's mark reports what was done to it. THE REDUCTION From the cartoon to the emblem in four steps, each one a frame. Every step keeps the three things that make it Bolas: a round body, legs that spread down, and a red line from above. 1 · CHARACTER the cartoon: for films, end cards, stories 2 · FLAT no shading, straight legs: for signage and print 3 · EMBLEM O over A: the professional mark 4 · MINIMAL line, O, A, nothing else: for stamps and small use THE SPIDER ENGINEER BECOMES OA Hanging from its line, a spider's silhouette is already two letters: the round abdomen is an O, the legs spreading down make an A. The red line comes from above, and, as in your OA mark, one leg of the A is red: the operation completes the letter. THE EMBLEM Read top to bottom: a red line, an O, an A. Read whole: a spider hanging from its thread. The A's red leg is the same stroke as in the OA logotype. THE LOGOTYPE, HUNG The horizontal OA keeps its red leg; a thread drops onto the O and two eyes appear in it. The wordmark is a spider waiting on its line. EIGHT LEGS, ONE A The A's two strokes multiply into eight legs, four a side. The outermost right leg stays red: one leg of eight does the operation. O A SET IN TYPE With the house condensed face: an O stacked on an A under a red line. Works anywhere a logo cannot be drawn. WAYS TO READ IT One mark, several readings, and none of them is the final one. Put it next to different things and it becomes a different instrument. That is the lab's own thesis, held in a single drawing. A SPIDER on its thread, waiting to drop into a shot O A TWO LETTERS the Operative Archive, abbreviated A PLAYHEAD standing on a film's timeline, at the moment now A PLUMB LINE the engineer's weight on a string: a true vertical to measure against A PENDULUM time kept by swinging: the cut as a beat A HANGING LAMP lighting the one frame under it A BOOM MICROPHONE lowered to listen: the sound passes A CURSOR the pointer that has just dropped into the archive SCALES Each size gets its own draw

lab/bolas/webs-that-matter.html.text: Bolas set 12 / 14 ← Bolas Pixel The Web of Cineosis → CINEOSIS LAB · BOLAS · WEBS THAT MATTER Webs That Matter Bateson called information “a difference which makes a difference.” Here every sign is drawn as its defining difference, and every film's web is spun from that film's own data. Nothing on this page is decoration. Each strand is a number the lab measured. The table of signs, as one web Forty-five signs in their places on the table. Each red thread is a confusion the lab recorded: two signs that get taken for each other. Click a sign to see it beside the three it is confused with, and the difference that tells them apart. SIGN 1 · So Solid perception One body owns the frame: either we see through its eyes (POV, eyelid/mask/windscreen framing) or we see it held at the hub with everything else arranged around it — and the image would lose its organising centre if that body were removed. SIGN 2 · Lq · CONFUSED WITH Liquid perception The centre moves: in a continuous reframing the shot passes from one character or environment to another, each central only until the next captures the screen. SIGN 4 · Ic · CONFUSED WITH Icon The face is not a feature of a person in a space but the whole image: a close-up in which expression (fixed wonder or traversing micro-movements) holds an intensity that has not yet become action. SIGN 34a · Op · CONFUSED WITH Opsign With the sound off, is the image something to be seen and nothing more: no one's goal organises it, what moves in it resolves nothing, and the look is not converted into action? The films, spun from their data Bolas spins each web, strand by strand, from what that film actually measured. The same web, drawn at 32 pixels, is the film's favicon, so the icon is the data too. lab/datacard.html.text: Cineosis Lab · Data Card WHAT KIND OF ARCHIVE IS THIS? EXPLAINERS ATLAS PAPERS CINEOSIS LAB · DATA CARD · as of 16 October 2026 · numbers from the lab’s own records (ledger.py) What kind of archive is this? The film, about four minutes. Open it full screen. An operative counter-reading of a public archive. A database made intentional by its questions; a taxonomy, and a zoo of shots out of their films; an archive that acts on what it holds. Not, yet, a counter-archive. THE WORDS Six words, kept strict WORD WHAT IT IS THE LAB BECAUSE Collection Things of one kind, gathered with some coherence YES 15,149 shots: each a few seconds cut from a film, with an in and an out Database Records you can query, with no order of their own; every query makes one (Manovich: database against narrative) YES 366 questions from the 45 signs, about 8.1 each; vectors from CLIP and DINO; every finder in the Atlas is a query Catalogue A database about works, as IMDb is: it describes, it does not hold PARTLY The lab describes 1,420 films it does not own; it holds copies of 1,731 shots Taxonomy A scheme that sorts things into kinds YES The 45 signs of the cineosis, in eight families, laid over every shot Zoo Specimens taken out of their habitat and shown by kind YES Each shot is shown away from its film; its source and seconds are kept, its surroundings are not Archive, strictly Records kept on purpose by someone with a mandate and custody, in their original order (Derrida’s arkheion: a beginning and a command) NO No custody of originals, no mandate, no original order: a layer of questions over the Moving Image Archive Operative archive An archive that acts: it computes, sorts and makes (Ernst; Farocki’s operational images) YES It searches, scores, sieves and cuts; the films it makes are its output Counter-archive A situated practice against a dominant record: it exposes absence, misdescription and exclusion, and its politics live in governance, circulation, transparency and the authority to revise or withhold PARTLY See below: counter to use and to machine authority; not in governance Two more ideas belong to this lab.
